headline: Claims counterexamples to strong forms of Arnold's fixed-point conjecture; the three-point quadric example is in Lean.
scope: Specific closed symplectic manifolds: the complex quadric threefold, twelve-dimensional examples, and simply connected Kähler manifolds of real dimension 22 and 3332.
plain: Arnold's conjecture links two counts: fixed points of a mechanical motion on a space, and critical points of a function on it. Strong forms predict that any such motion has at least as many fixed points as some topological count. Five papers build spaces where these strong forms fail. The cleanest example is a motion on a six-dimensional quadric with only three fixed points, where any function needs four. Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of that example.
doesNot: This does not disprove the homological, Floer-theoretic lower bounds for nondegenerate fixed points; the papers present their examples as compatible with those bounds. Only the quadric example has a Lean statement.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Vladimir Arnold, who posed the fixed-point questions
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims counterexamples to several standard strong forms of Arnold's conjecture, one of them with a Lean statement.

explanation:
Take a round sphere and turn it a small angle about its vertical axis. Only the north and south poles stay put, so this motion has two fixed points. Now take the height function on the sphere. Its critical points, where the slope is zero, are the top and the bottom, again two. This is no accident. For a short motion made from a function this way, the fixed points are exactly the function's critical points[1]. A motion of this kind, generated by an energy function as in classical mechanics, is a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism.

Arnold's conjecture asks whether every Hamiltonian diffeomorphism keeps at least the minimum number of critical points forced by the topology[2]. There are several ways to count that minimum. The critical number counts critical points of any smooth function. The Morse number allows only well-behaved, nondegenerate functions. The stable Morse number also allows extra auxiliary variables[3]. Conley and Zehnder proved the torus case, and Fortune proved a bound on complex projective space[4]. Floer's methods gave lower bounds from homology, a tool that counts holes[5].

The fifth paper gives the cleanest example. On the complex quadric threefold, a six-dimensional space cut out by one equation, it builds a motion with exactly three fixed points. Every smooth function there has at least four critical points[6]. At least one fixed point is degenerate, meaning not well-behaved[7]. The count of three is sharp, because Gong had already shown that every such motion on this space has at least three fixed points[8].

The other papers handle the nondegenerate versions, where every fixed point is well-behaved. The fourth paper builds a twelve-dimensional example with fewer fixed points than the Morse number[9]. The third gives a space with sixteen fewer fixed points than its stable Morse number[10]. The first makes the gap grow without limit in dimension 22. For each m it builds a space with stable Morse number 80 + 1968m and a motion with 80 + 1952m fixed points[11]. For m = 1 that is 2048 against 2032, a gap of 16. For m = 10 it is 19760 against 19600, a gap of 160. The ratio 2032/2048 is exactly 127/128. The second paper, in dimension 3332, has 1,872,232 fixed points against a stable Morse number of 1,872,264, a gap of exactly 32[12]. The key idea is torsion. It is a finer part of homology that appears only when holes are counted with whole numbers, not fractions. Torsion can force more critical points than the count of holes taken with fractions[13]. These examples show that fixed points need not feel that extra pressure.

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of the quadric example: three fixed points, while every function has at least four. So the fifth paper proves that result, as far as the Lean statement matches the paper. The nondegenerate constructions are not in the Lean scope. They remain claims. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: Major. The quadric counterexample has a Lean statement; the nondegenerate constructions in very high dimensions are claims only. Floer-theoretic forms of Arnold's conjecture are untouched. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: The result of running, for one unit of time, a motion generated by a changing energy function.
A point that a map sends to itself.
A point where a function's slope is zero in every direction.
Well-behaved: for a fixed point, its linear part has no eigenvalue 1.
The least number of critical points of a function whose critical points are all nondegenerate.
The Morse number when extra variables with a fixed quadratic shape far out are allowed.
A space with a rule for signed area in pairs of directions, the setting of classical mechanics.
Parts of homology that vanish when counted with fractions but matter when counted with whole numbers.

claims.text: The stable Morse number is the least number of critical points of Morse functions on W × R^k that are quadratic at infinity.
claims.sourceQuote: Its \emph{stable Morse number} $\SM(W)$ is the minimum of $\#\Crit(F)$ over integers $k\geq0$ and smooth Morse functions $F:W\times\R^k\to\R$ such that, for $k>0$, \[ F(x,z)=Q(z)\qquad\text{for all sufficiently large }|z|, \] where $Q$ is a nondegenerate quadratic form of arbitrary signature.
